results.evidence: Post uses general language throughout ('The Sixth Amendment', 'under their jurisdiction's rules', 'constitutionally required') — no specific statute numbers appear.

Post cites only organizations (NACDL, ABA, NLADA, Bureau of Justice Statistics) and anonymous references ('One criminal justice researcher', 'legal researchers and former federal prosecutors') — no individual attorney or legal scholar names appear.

All statistics are sourced: 97% federal pleas and 94% state pleas (Bureau of Justice Statistics; NACDL), 3-6x sentencing differential (NACDL 'The Trial Penalty' report), 200-500+ caseloads (NLADA/ABA public defender caseload studies). Narrative numbers ('eleven minutes', 'two years probation') are clearly hypothetical scene-setting, not factual claims.

All procedural claims are jurisdiction-qualified: 'in most states' (fee arbitration), 'In every state' (bar complaints), 'virtually any stage' (firing attorney), 'under their jurisdiction's rules' (discovery). No bare universal deadlines or filing requirements appear.
Only 'Brady' references appear (Brady material, Brady demand, Brady violations, Brady requires it) — all fall within the allowed legal-terminology exceptions. No other case citations found.

No collateral-consequence claims (licensing, housing, firearms, voting, immigration) appear. References to 'employment uncertainty', 'relationship strain', and 'lose income' describe pretrial effects of ongoing cases, not post-conviction collateral consequences.

results.reason: Frontmatter has no question_count field to mismatch; body contains 7 clear attorney questions (one per section) plus the consolidated list, which is internally consistent.
Major factual claims are sourced inline (NACDL Trial Penalty report, Bureau of Justice Statistics, ABA/NLADA caseload studies, Brady doctrine).
Action items use plain imperatives ('Ask this today,' 'Write the number down,' 'Copy these seven questions') and any legal terms are immediately explained in context.
None of the flagged cliches ('end of the day,' 'tip of the iceberg,' 'slippery slope,' 'double-edged sword,' 'game changer,' 'wake-up call') appear in the post.

Section 2 contains a 5-sentence run in third person ('Cases move through at volume. Attorneys can't review every document. Motions don't get filed. Witnesses don't get interviewed. Defendants plead.') that drops the 'you' voice longer than the 2-sentence tolerance.
Passive constructions appear occasionally ('is documented,' 'are disclosed') but well under 30% of sentences; most action sentences use active voice.
'Trial penalty,' 'Brady material,' and 'bar complaint' are defined on first use, but 'motion to compel,' 'suppression motion,' and 'fee arbitration' appear without immediate definition.
Logical arc: TLDR overview, scenario intro, seven numbered realities each with context and a paired question, then consolidated question list and CTA — no orphaned paragraphs.
Multiple actionable next steps: 7 attorney questions, free Case Progress Score link, Case Decoder product link, and specific 'do this today' instructions in every section.
Action instructions are direct imperatives ('Ask this,' 'Write it down,' 'Bookmark it'); hedges like 'likely' and 'may' appear only in informational statements about outcomes, which is allowed.
No paragraph approaches 300 words; action-oriented paragraphs are consistently short (under 100 words) and often just 2-3 sentences.
The seven numbered sections are roughly comparable in length; no single section dominates more than ~20% of total word count.

Each threat (trial penalty sentence multipliers, public defender overload, lost time during continuances, hidden discovery, bad plea offers) is immediately followed by a specific attorney question or concrete action within 1-2 sentences.

Opens with a vivid 2AM scenario and stark stat (3-6x trial penalty, 97% pleas), builds with 7 documented realities and cited evidence, closes with a consolidated 7-question script and bookmark-now instructions.

results.evidence: Post frames actions as questions to ask your attorney rather than directives; e.g., 'Question to ask your attorney' format throughout.
Every one of the 7 sections ends with a 'Question to ask your attorney' redirect, keeping counsel in the loop proximate to each decision topic.
Post speaks generally about structural realities and never evaluates the reader's specific case strength or likely outcome.
Motions like Brady demands and motions to compel are described generally and framed as questions to ask the attorney ('Have you filed a Brady demand?'), not as steps the reader should take.
Post contains no discussion of immigration, deportation, visa, or green card consequences, so the immigration redirect requirement is not triggered.
Caseload claims attributed to 'NLADA/ABA public defender caseload studies' and trial penalty figures attributed to 'NACDL — The Trial Penalty report' and 'Bureau of Justice Statistics.'
Post references only general categories like 'public defenders,' 'prosecutors,' and 'bar association' — no specific firm or company is named as a recommendation.
Post avoids 'we recommend' phrasing; the only first-person plural usage is 'We provide research, analysis, and questions' in the disclaimer, not a legal-action recommendation.

Narrative vignettes at the start of each section are written in second person as illustrative framing ('You're sitting in a holding area') and are clearly generalized rather than presented as real case facts.

Closing disclaimer states 'We provide research, analysis, and questions to help you work more effectively with your attorney,' framing information as empowerment to ask better questions, not self-representation.
Uses qualifiers like 'typically,' 'in some jurisdictions,' 'in most states,' and 'depends on your specific facts' when describing legal rules.
Post explicitly says 'that depends on your specific facts' and frames outcomes as variable; no guarantees that following the advice produces a specific result.
Strategies and claims are attributed to NACDL's 'The Trial Penalty' report, ABA/NLADA caseload standards, Brady doctrine, and Bureau of Justice Statistics.
TLDRBox says public defenders carry '300-500+ cases' while FAQ says '200-500+ cases' — a minor numeric inconsistency, but not a contradictory legal claim about the law itself.

Case Decoder and Case Progress Score are framed as tools for 'a clear analysis of your specific case' and 'research, analysis, and questions to help you work more effectively with your attorney,' not as substitutes for representation.

Opening starts with system description ('The criminal justice system has no instruction manual for defendants') rather than naming the reader's fear, and H2s are declarative/topical ('The Trial Penalty Is Real', 'Discovery Is Leverage', 'Judge Patterns Are Publicly Available') rather than action-oriented 'how to' framing.
'Brady material' is defined inline but 'suppression motions', 'fee arbitration', and 'Sixth Amendment' appear without inline definitions; paragraph lengths stay within 4 sentences.

TLDRBox contains a 'Your Next Step' action block before the first H2, but the action is 'Ask your attorney...' which requires an attorney meeting rather than a sub-5-minute action completable alone on a phone.
Each section presents one recommended action (a specific question to ask the attorney) with UPL-safe framing and a clear default path, no 3+ option decision points.
Section 7 'What most defendants don't know' presents a bulleted list of 4 items (bar complaint, fee arbitration, fire attorney, request case file) without 'start with these' priority markers.
This post uses the system-decoder-post pattern — enumerated structural realities of how the system operates, each paired with a decoder question.

The '3-6x longer sentences' statistic in Section 1 is followed by 'But here's what nobody mentions' commentary rather than an immediate paired action; the question/action arrives much later at the end of the section.
Zero blame language; the post consistently frames problems as structural ('underfunding isn't an accident', 'the prosecution has no incentive') and never implies the reader caused their situation.

Opening launches into system description without validating the reader's fear emotionally; the middle reduces unknown to known well and the final body line 'The act of reading them out loud changes the conversation' is agency-forward, but the post ends on a generic tier CTA box rather than an agency statement.

No tables and only H2 headings used, but Sections 1, 2, and 7 run close to or over 500 words before the next H2, and the bulleted question subsections in 4 and 6 push section length past the phone-friendly target.

Every H2 section contains exactly one standalone bolded sentence under 27 words that is shareable, e.g. 'A constitutional right without the funding to exercise it is a constitutional decoration' and 'Information asymmetry is a choice the system makes — and every question you ask reverses it.'

Both FAQ answers start with the direct answer (no hedging preamble), stay within 2-4 sentences, and read as informed-peer voice rather than institutional ('The system is designed for efficiency, not individual justice. 97% of federal cases end in pleas...').
